## Checking balance {background-color="#23373B"}

- Model-level diagnostics
- Variable-level diagnostics
- Balance across the joint distribution

## Model-level diagnostics {background-color="#23373B"}

Before weighting, we checked the calibration, the ROC curve, and the AUC of the propensity score model

Now: did weighting remove what the model knew?

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true

library(halfmoon)
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(causalworkshop)
library(propensity)
library(scales)

propensity_model <- glm(
  net ~ income + health + temperature,
  family = binomial(),
  data = net_data
)

net_data_wts <- propensity_model |>
  augment(type.predict = "response", data = net_data) |>
  mutate(w_ate = wt_ate(.fitted, net))
```

## Weighted ROC curve ![](img/hex/halfmoon.png){.absolute top=0 right=0 width=140}

<br />
<br />

If the weights did their job, the model should no longer discriminate between the exposure groups

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"
#| output-location: slide

net_data_wts |>
  check_model_roc_curve(net, .fitted, .weights = w_ate) |>
  plot_model_roc_curve()
```

## Weighted AUC

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

check_model_auc(
  net_data_wts,
  .exposure = net,
  .fitted = .fitted,
  .weights = w_ate
)
```

## Weighted AUC

- In a prediction model, a weighted AUC of 0.50 would be a failure
- In a causal model, it means the confounders no longer tell the groups apart

## Effective sample size {background-color="#23373B"}

$$\LARGE ESS = \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i^2}$$

The approximate number of independent observations after weighting

## Effective sample size in R

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

net_data_wts |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    ess_ate = ess(w_ate),
    percent_ess = percent(ess_ate / n)
  )
```

. . .

Weighting buys balance at the price of precision

## ESS by exposure group

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

net_data_wts |>
  group_by(net) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    ess_ate = ess(w_ate),
    percent_ess = percent(ess_ate / n)
  )
```

. . .

The grouped values do not sum to the total: each measures the variation in a different set of weights

## Where does the variation come from?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot(net_data_wts, aes(x = as.numeric(w_ate), fill = factor(net))) +
  geom_density(color = NA) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "ATE weight", fill = "Net use")
```

## The price of balance

- Weighting introduces variation, so precision drops
- The more variable the weights, the lower the ESS
- If the ESS is too small: different weights, or trimming and truncation

## Comparing weights with ESS

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-7|9-10"
#| output-location: slide

net_data_wts <- net_data_wts |>
  mutate(
    w_att = wt_att(.fitted, net),
    w_atu = wt_atu(.fitted, net),
    w_atm = wt_atm(.fitted, net),
    w_ato = wt_ato(.fitted, net)
  )

net_data_wts |>
  plot_ess(.weights = starts_with("w_"))
```

. . .

When several sets of weights answer your question, all else being equal, pick the one with the highest ESS

## Variable-level diagnostics {background-color="#23373B"}

Exchangeability means the groups are exchangeable *within levels of the confounders*

A consequence: exchangeable groups are balanced at the variable level

## Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) {background-color="#23373B"}

$$\LARGE d = \frac{\bar{x}_{treatment}-\bar{x}_{control}}{\sqrt{\frac{s^2_{treatment}+s^2_{control}}{2}}}$$

## Balance in R ![](img/hex/halfmoon.png){.absolute top=0 right=0 width=140}

<br />
<br />

Calculate standardized mean differences and other balance metrics

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|4|6|7|8"

library(halfmoon)
library(tidyverse)

balance_metrics <- check_balance(
  df,
  .vars = c(confounder_1, confounder_2, ...),
  .exposure = exposure,
  .weights = wts # optional
)
```

## Calculating balance metrics

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| eval: true

vars <- c("income", "health", "temperature")

balance_metrics <- check_balance(
  net_data_wts,
  .vars = all_of(vars),
  .exposure = net,
  .weights = w_ate
)

balance_metrics
```

## Standardized mean differences

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: slide

smds <- balance_metrics |>
  filter(metric == "smd")

smds
```

---

## Plotting SMDs ![](img/hex/halfmoon.png){.absolute top=0 right=0 width=140}

<br />

Plot them! (in a Love plot!)

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|2|3-8|10"

ggplot(
  data = smds,
  aes(
    x = abs(estimate),
    y = variable,
    group = method,
    color = method
  )
) +
  geom_love()
```

## Love plot

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot(
  data = smds,
  aes(x = abs(estimate), y = variable, group = method, color = method)
) +
  geom_love()
```

## Variance ratios

The ratio of the within-group variances, ideally as close to 1 as possible

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2|8"
#| output-location: slide

vrs <- balance_metrics |>
  filter(metric == "vr")

ggplot(
  data = vrs,
  aes(x = estimate, y = variable, group = method, color = method)
) +
  geom_love(vline_xintercept = 1)
```

### Create a Love Plot for the propensity score weighting you created in the previous exercise

## Unweighted boxplot

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: slide

ggplot(
  net_data_wts,
  aes(x = factor(net), y = income, color = factor(net))
) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.color = NA, fill = NA, width = 0.3, color = "black") +
  labs(color = "Net use", y = "Income", x = NULL)
```

## Weighted boxplot

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|3"
#| output-location: slide

ggplot(
  net_data_wts,
  aes(x = factor(net), y = income, color = factor(net), weight = w_ate)
) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.color = NA, fill = NA, width = 0.3, color = "black") +
```

## Many geoms accept weights {.small}

Treat the weighted pseudo-population as a real sample and make good use of your exploratory data analysis skills

`geom_bar()`, `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_contour()`, `geom_count()`, `geom_density()`, `geom_dotplot()`, `geom_freqpoly()`, `geom_hex()`, `geom_histogram()`, `geom_quantile()`, `geom_smooth()`, `geom_violin()`

## ECDF

For continuous variables, it can be helpful to look at the _whole_ distribution pre and post-weighting rather than a single summary measure

## ECDF

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

ggplot(net_data_wts, aes(x = income, color = factor(net))) +
  geom_ecdf() +
  scale_color_manual(
    "Net use",
    values = c("#5154B8", "#5DB854"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  xlab("Income") +
  ylab("Proportion <= x")
```

## Unweighted ECDF

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|2"
#| eval: true
#| output-location: slide

ggplot(net_data_wts, aes(x = income, color = factor(net))) +
  geom_ecdf() +
  scale_color_manual(
    "Net use",
    values = c("#5154B8", "#5DB854"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  xlab("Income") +
  ylab("Proportion <= x")
```

## Weighted  ECDF

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"
#| output-location: slide

ggplot(net_data_wts, aes(x = income, color = factor(net))) +
  geom_ecdf(aes(weights = w_ate)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    "Net use",
    values = c("#5154B8", "#5DB854"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  xlab("Income") +
  ylab("Proportion <= x (Weighted)")
```

## Weighted ECDF for temperature

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1"
#| output-location: slide

ggplot(net_data_wts, aes(x = temperature, color = factor(net))) +
  geom_ecdf(aes(weights = w_ate)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    "Net use",
    values = c("#5154B8", "#5DB854"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  xlab("Temperature") +
  ylab("Proportion <= x (Weighted)")
```

## A non-linear relationship

- The weighted curves overlap until about 27 degrees, then they diverge
- The SMD for temperature is near zero, so it would have missed this
- Let's refit the propensity score model with a natural spline

## Refit with a spline

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"

propensity_model_ns <- glm(
  net ~ income + health + splines::ns(temperature, df = 5),
  family = binomial(),
  data = net_data
)

net_data_ns <- propensity_model_ns |>
  augment(type.predict = "response", data = net_data) |>
  mutate(w_ate = wt_ate(.fitted, net))
```

## Weighted ECDF with the spline

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot(net_data_ns, aes(x = temperature, color = factor(net))) +
  geom_ecdf(aes(weights = w_ate)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    "Net use",
    values = c("#5154B8", "#5DB854"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  xlab("Temperature") +
  ylab("Proportion <= x (Weighted)")
```

## Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic

The maximum vertical distance between the two ECDF curves

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|7"
#| output-location: slide

check_balance(
  net_data_ns,
  .vars = all_of(vars),
  .exposure = net,
  .weights = w_ate
) |>
  filter(metric == "ks")
```

We care about the magnitude, not the hypothesis test

## Balance across the joint distribution {background-color="#23373B"}

Exchangeability requires balance across the *joint* distribution of the confounders

That includes interactions between variables and higher moments

## Interactions and squares

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|6-7|10-12"
#| output-location: slide

balance_metrics_joint <- check_balance(
  net_data_ns,
  .vars = all_of(vars),
  .exposure = net,
  .weights = w_ate,
  interactions = TRUE,
  squares = TRUE
)

balance_metrics_joint |>
  filter(metric %in% c("smd", "vr")) |>
  plot_balance(facet_scales = "free_x")
```

## Refit with an interaction

`income_x_health` is the least balanced product term, and the propensity score model does not include that interaction

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"

propensity_model_int <- glm(
  net ~ income * health + splines::ns(temperature, df = 5),
  family = binomial(),
  data = net_data
)

net_data_int <- propensity_model_int |>
  augment(type.predict = "response", data = net_data_ns) |>
  mutate(w_int = wt_ate(.fitted, net))
```

## Balance with the interaction

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|5"
#| output-location: slide

check_balance(
  net_data_int,
  .vars = all_of(vars),
  .exposure = net,
  .weights = c(w_ate, w_int),
  interactions = TRUE,
  squares = TRUE
) |>
  filter(variable == "income_x_health", metric %in% c("ks", "vr"))
```

An interaction in the propensity score model fixes an imbalanced product term, just as the spline fixed temperature

## Energy

The average distance across the joint ECDFs: one number for the whole covariate space

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

balance_metrics_joint |>
  filter(metric == "energy") |>
  select(method, estimate)
```

. . .

The scale depends on the confounders, so use energy to compare approaches

## Don't use p-values

- Balance is a property of the *sample*; p-values refer to a hypothetical population
- p-values depend on sample size: dropping observations at random "improves" them
- There is no theoretical link between a p-value cut-off and good balance

::: tiny
Imai, King, and Stuart (2008)
:::

## Balancing weights {background-color="#23373B"}

- So far, we modeled the propensity score, then checked whether its weights balance

- An alternative approach is to directly optimize the weights to achieve balance without explicitly modeling the propensity score

## Optimizing the energy statistic

- We used the energy statistic to measure balance across the joint distribution

- Energy balancing weights minimize it directly

## Energy balancing weights

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|6|7"
#| output-location: slide

library(balancing)

energy_fit <- balance(
  net_data_ns,
  .exposure = net,
  .covariates = c(income, health, temperature),
  method = bw_energy(),
  estimand = "ate"
)

energy_fit
```

## Extracting the weights

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: slide

net_data_ns <- net_data_ns |>
  mutate(w_energy = weights(energy_fit))

ggplot(net_data_ns, aes(x = w_energy)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)
```

## Comparing balance metrics

```{r}
#| eval: true

balance_metrics_energy <- check_balance(
  net_data_ns,
  .vars = all_of(vars),
  .exposure = net,
  .weights = c(w_ate, w_energy),
  interactions = TRUE,
  squares = TRUE
)
```

## Comparing energy

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

balance_metrics_energy |>
  filter(metric == "energy") |>
  select(method, estimate)
```

. . .

Lower energy than the spline model we tuned by hand

## Comparing SMDs

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: slide

balance_metrics_energy |>
  filter(metric == "smd") |>
  plot_balance()
```

## Weighted ECDF with energy weights

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"
#| output-location: slide

ggplot(net_data_ns, aes(x = temperature, color = factor(net))) +
  geom_ecdf(aes(weights = w_energy)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    "Net use",
    values = c("#5154B8", "#5DB854"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  xlab("Temperature") +
  ylab("Proportion <= x (Weighted)")
```

The optimization balanced the whole distribution, with no spline needed

## Energy weights and ESS

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

net_data_ns |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    ess_ate = ess(w_ate),
    ess_energy = ess(w_energy)
  )
```

. . .

Better joint balance did not cost effective sample size here

## Other balancing weights {.small}

  | Weights                              | Function       | What it optimizes                                         |
  | ------------------------------------ | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Entropy                              | `bw_entropy()` | Uniformity of the weights, with exact mean balance        |
  | Inverse probability tilting          | `bw_ipt()`     | A propensity model tilted to match the weighted means     |
  | Covariate balancing propensity score | `bw_cbps()`    | A propensity score that also satisfies balance conditions |
  | Energy                               | `bw_energy()`  | The energy distance across the joint distribution         |
  | Kernel distance                      | `bw_cfd()`     | A kernel distance between the weighted groups             |
  | Stable                               | `bw_sbw()`     | Weight variability, holding means within a tolerance      |

All are fit the same way through `balance()`; only `method` changes

## Inference with balancing weights

- Energy, kernel distance, and stable weights have no analytic standard errors, so bootstrap, refitting the weights in each resample

  | `ipw()`        | Bootstrap     |
  | -------------- | ------------- |
  | `bw_entropy()` | `bw_energy()` |
  | `bw_ipt()`     | `bw_cfd()`    |
  | `bw_cbps()`    | `bw_sbw()`    |

## `ipw()` with balancing weights

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-6|8-12|14"

entropy_fit <- balance(
  net_data_ns,
  .exposure = net,
  .covariates = c(income, health, temperature),
  method = bw_entropy()
)

outcome_model <- lm(
  malaria_risk ~ net,
  data = net_data_ns,
  weights = weights(entropy_fit)
)

ipw_fit <- ipw(entropy_fit, outcome_model)
```

## `ipw()` with balancing weights {.small}

```{r}
#| eval: true

ipw_fit
```

### *Bonus!* Weighted Tables in R

## 1. Create a "design object" to incorporate the weights {.gtsummary}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(survey)

svy_des <- svydesign(
  ids = ~1,
  data = df,
  weights = ~wts
)
```

## 2. Pass to `gtsummary::tbl_svysummary()` {.gtsummary}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(gtsummary)
tbl_svysummary(svy_des, by = x) |>
  add_ess_header() |>
  add_overall(last = TRUE)
```

## {.gtsummary .tiny}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| eval: true
#| echo: false

library(survey)
library(gtsummary)

svy_des <- svydesign(
  ids = ~1,
  data = net_data_wts |>
    select(income, health, temperature, w_ate, net) |>
    mutate(net = factor(net, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))),
  weights = ~w_ate
)
theme_gtsummary_compact()

tbl_svysummary(svy_des, by = net, include = c(income, health, temperature)) |>
  add_ess_header() |>
  add_overall(last = TRUE)
```
